children.value: The null and alternative hypotheses for the z-test for the population mean (μ) have exactly the same structure as the hypotheses for the z-test for the population proportion (p):
The null hypothesis has the form

children.html: H0:μ=μ0H_0: \mu = \mu_0H0​:μ=μ0​
μ0\mu_0μ0​

children.value: The alternative hypothesis takes one of the following three forms (depending on the context):

children.html: Ha:μ<μ0H_a: \mu < \mu_0Ha​:μ<μ0​
Ha:μ>μ0H_a: \mu > \mu_0Ha​:μ>μ0​

children.value: Example 1: SAT-M Scores at Ross College

In our example 1, based on a sample of 4 students from Ross College, we were testing whether the mean SAT-M of all Ross College students is higher than the national mean (which, by construction, is 500). The hypotheses are therefore:

children.html: H0:μ=500H_0: \mu = 500H0​:μ=500
Ha:μ>500H_a: \mu > 500Ha​:μ>500

model.question: A tire manufacturer advertises that its tires last an average of 50,000 miles. A consumer group suspects the true average is lower. What are the appropriate hypotheses?

choices.feedback: Correct! H₀: μ = 50,000 vs. Hₐ: μ < 50,000.
The suspicion is specifically that tires last less, so the alternative is one-sided.
The null hypothesis always states equality with the null value.

model.hint: The advertised value is the null value; the group suspects LOWER.

children.value: Example 2: Concentration of a Chemical in a Drug

Here we want to test whether the mean concentration of a certain chemical in a large shipment of a certain prescription drug is the required 250 ppm. Since a concentration that is too high OR too low is a problem, the null and alternative hypotheses in this case are:

children.html: H0:μ=250H_0: \mu = 250H0​:μ=250
Ha:μ≠250H_a: \mu \neq 250Ha​:μ=250

children.value: All inference procedures are based on probability. We are trying to determine if our sample results are likely or unlikely based on our assumptions about the population. This requires a probability model that describes the long-term behavior of sample results randomly collected from a population that fits our hypothesis. For this reason, the Central Limit Theorem gives us criteria for deciding if the z-test for the population mean can be used. We need to verify that (i) the sample is random (or at least can be considered random in context), and (ii) we are in one of the “OK” situations in the following table:
Conditions: z-test for a population mean
Variable varies normally in the population
Variable doesn’t vary normally in the population
If the conditions are met, then

children.html: Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ

children.value: values vary normally, or at least close enough to normally to use a normal model to calculate probabilities. When

children.html: Xˉ\bar{X}Xˉ

children.value: values are normal, the z-scores will be normally distributed with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1.
Let’s go back to our examples.

The variable of interest, SAT-M scores, is assumed to vary normally in the population, so the fact that the sample size is small (n = 4) is not a problem (“variable varies normally, small sample size”—OK). Sample means will be normally distributed, and we can use a normal probability model based on z-scores to determine probabilities.

children.value: In this case, the conditions that allow us to carry out the z-test are met since:

The sample size (n = 100) is large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to apply (“variable doesn’t necessarily vary normally, large sample size”—OK; note that in this case the large sample is essential, since the concentration level is not known to vary normally).
The z-statistic in this case is:

children.html: z=247−25012100=−2.5z=\frac{247-250}{\frac{12}{\sqrt{100}}}=-2.5z=100​12​247−250​=−2.5

children.value: Our data (represented by the sample mean concentration level, 247) are 2.5 standard deviations below the null value. A difference of 2.5 standard deviations is considered quite strong evidence against

children.html: H0H_0H0​

children.value: . (Essentially any difference that is above 2 standard deviations is considered quite large.) This will be confirmed when we find the p-value of the test.
Check Your Understanding: Checking Conditions and the Test Statistic

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Checking Conditions and the Test Statistic

children.value: Normal body temperature for healthy, at-rest human beings has long been said to be 98.6°F. A doctor has seen many patients who had a lower or higher body temperature when they were not ill. He has read research that says it is actually lower. So he collected 50 randomly selected temperatures, which had a mean of 98.4°F. The standard deviation is known to be 0.35°F. He tests

children.html: H0:μ=98.6H_0: \mu = 98.6H0​:μ=98.6
Ha:μ≠98.6H_a: \mu \neq 98.6Ha​:μ=98.6

model.question: Are the conditions for the z-test met, and what is the test statistic?

choices.feedback: Correct! The sample is random and n = 50 is large enough for the CLT, so the test is safe. z = −0.2/0.0495 ≈ −4.04.
Check the standard error: 0.35/√50 ≈ 0.0495, so z ≈ −4.04, not −0.57.

choices.text: Conditions are not met because we don't know that body temperature is normally distributed
choices.feedback: The large sample size (50 > 30) means normality of body temperatures is not required.

model.question: A test statistic of z ≈ −4.04 means the sample mean is more than 4 standard deviations below 98.6. What should the doctor anticipate about the p-value?

choices.text: The p-value will be very small—strong evidence that mean body temperature differs from 98.6°F
choices.feedback: Correct! Values beyond ±4 standard deviations are extremely rare under H₀, so the p-value will be tiny (about 0.00005) and the result highly significant.

choices.text: The p-value will be large, since the test statistic is negative
choices.feedback: It's the opposite—the more extreme the test statistic, the SMALLER the p-value.

children.value: Check Your Understanding: Conditions for the z-Test for a Mean

children.label: Check Your Understanding: Conditions for the z-Test for a Mean

children.value: Each histogram below represents a random sample. We do not know if the variable is distributed normally in the population, but we want to be reasonably sure that the distribution of sample means will be normal so that we can use the z-test for testing claims about the population mean.

model.question: A histogram of a sample of n = 15 observations is clearly skewed to the right, suggesting the variable may not be normal in the population. How should we proceed with a z-test for μ?

choices.text: Do not use the z-test—the sample is small and the variable does not appear to vary normally
choices.feedback: Correct! With a small sample (15 < 30) and evidence of non-normality, we are in the "NOT OK" cell—sample means can't be assumed normal, so the z-test should not be used.

choices.text: Use the z-test—the Central Limit Theorem applies
choices.feedback: 15 is well below the n > 30 guideline, so the CLT cannot rescue us here.

choices.text: Use the z-test—the histogram shows the population is normal enough
choices.feedback: The skewed histogram suggests the population is NOT normal, so we cannot rely on that condition.

model.hint: Small sample + variable that doesn't appear to vary normally—check the conditions table.

model.question: A histogram of a sample of n = 250 observations is moderately skewed. How should we proceed with a z-test for μ?

choices.text: Use the z-test—the sample is large enough for the Central Limit Theorem to apply
choices.feedback: Correct! With n = 250, the Central Limit Theorem guarantees that sample means are approximately normal even though the variable itself is skewed—the z-test is fine.

choices.text: Do not use the z-test—the variable is skewed
choices.feedback: Normality of the VARIABLE isn't required when the sample is large; the CLT ensures the sample MEAN is approximately normal.
